title: Genetics and Evolution
lines: USAT-M Biology asks two kinds of genetics question: terms and facts (Mendel's laws, DNA structure, the genetic code, tools of biotechnology, theories of evolution) and short crosses that you solve with a Punnett square or a probability rule. Practise the crosses until each takes under a minute.
## Key terms
- Gene: a length of DNA that codes for one protein or trait. Alleles: different forms of the same gene, at the same place (locus) on a pair of chromosomes.
- Genotype: the alleles an organism has (TT, Tt, tt). Phenotype: the trait that shows (tall, dwarf).
- Homozygous: two identical alleles (TT or tt). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Tt).
- Dominant allele: shows its effect even in a heterozygote. Recessive allele: shows only when homozygous.
## Mendel's laws
Gregor Mendel, the father of genetics, worked with garden peas.
- Law of segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate, so each gamete gets only one.
- Law of independent assortment: genes on different chromosomes are sorted into gametes independently of each other.
| Cross | Phenotype ratio | Genotype ratio
| Tt × Tt (monohybrid) | 3 : 1 | 1 : 2 : 1
| Tt × tt (test cross) | 1 : 1 | 1 : 1
| RrYy × RrYy (dihybrid) | 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 | 9 genotypes
| RrYy × rryy (dihybrid test cross) | 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 | 1 : 1 : 1 : 1
A test cross mates an individual showing the dominant trait with a homozygous recessive. If any recessive offspring appear, the parent was heterozygous.
> In peas, round (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r). Two heterozygous plants are crossed and give 800 seeds. About how many seeds are wrinkled?
> Rr × Rr gives RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1, so ¼ are rr.
> ¼ × 800 = 200 wrinkled seeds.
- Number of gamete types = 2ⁿ, where n is the number of heterozygous gene pairs. AaBbCc gives 2³ = 8 types.
- To find the chance of one offspring type, split the cross into single genes and multiply. From RrYy × RrYy, the chance of rryy is ¼ × ¼ = 1/16.
## Beyond simple dominance
- Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is in between. In the four o'clock plant, red × white gives pink F₁, and the F₂ is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
- Codominance: both alleles show fully. Blood group AB shows both A and B antigens.
- Multiple alleles: the ABO gene has three alleles, IA, IB and i. IA and IB are codominant; both are dominant to i.
| Blood group | Possible genotypes
| A | IA IA or IA i
| B | IB IB or IB i
| AB | IA IB
| O | i i
> A man of group A (IA i) and a woman of group B (IB i) have a child. What are the chances of each blood group?
> Gametes: IA or i from the father; IB or i from the mother.
> Offspring: IA IB (AB), IA i (A), IB i (B), i i (O), each ¼.
> So all four groups are possible, each with probability ¼.
## Sex determination and sex linkage
- Humans have 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Females are XX, males XY. The father's sperm decides the sex of the child.
- Haemophilia and red-green colour blindness are X-linked recessive. A male has only one X, so one recessive allele is enough to show the disorder; this is why they are more common in males.
- A father passes his X to all daughters and his Y to all sons, so he never passes an X-linked allele to his son.
> A carrier woman (XH Xh) marries a man with normal blood clotting (XH Y). What fraction of their sons may have haemophilia?
> Sons receive Y from the father and one X from the mother: XH Y or Xh Y.
> Half of the sons may be haemophiliac. Daughters get XH from the father, so none is affected, but half are carriers.
! Read whether the question asks about sons, daughters or all children. Here ½ of sons are affected, but only ¼ of all children.
- Chromosome number disorders: Down syndrome (trisomy 21, 47 chromosomes), Klinefelter syndrome (XXY male), Turner syndrome (XO female, 45 chromosomes).
## DNA and protein synthesis

- Watson and Crick described the double helix in 1953, using X-ray work of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins. The two strands are antiparallel and are held by hydrogen bonds between bases: A with T, G with C.

- Replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule keeps one old strand (shown by Meselson and Stahl). DNA polymerase builds new strands only in the 5′ to 3′ direction, so the lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments, joined by DNA ligase.
- Transcription: DNA → mRNA in the nucleus; uracil replaces thymine. Translation: mRNA → protein on ribosomes; tRNA brings amino acids; rRNA forms part of the ribosome.

- The genetic code is a triplet code: 64 codons for 20 amino acids. It is degenerate (most amino acids have more than one codon) and almost universal. AUG is the start codon; UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.
> A DNA template strand reads TAC CGT. What mRNA is made from it?
> Pair each base: T → A, A → U, C → G, G → C.
> TAC → AUG and CGT → GCA, so the mRNA is AUG GCA. AUG is the start codon.
- A gene mutation is a change in the base sequence. In sickle-cell anaemia one base change replaces one amino acid in haemoglobin.
## Biotechnology
- Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific base sequences; DNA ligase joins pieces. A plasmid is the usual vector for carrying a gene into a bacterium.
- Recombinant DNA technology lets bacteria such as E. coli make human insulin and growth hormone.
- PCR (polymerase chain reaction) copies a piece of DNA many times using heat-stable Taq polymerase; after n cycles there are 2ⁿ copies.
- Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size; it is used in DNA fingerprinting for crime and paternity cases.
- Genetically modified crops include Bt cotton, which makes its own insecticidal protein. Dolly the sheep (1996) was the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell.
## Evolution
- Lamarck: use and disuse, and the inheritance of acquired characters. This idea is rejected.

- Darwin: natural selection (On the Origin of Species, 1859). Organisms overproduce; there is variation and a struggle for existence; those with favourable inherited variations survive and reproduce more. Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea independently.

- Evidence: fossils; homologous organs (same basic structure, different jobs, such as the forelimbs of a human, bat and whale) show common ancestry; analogous organs (same job, different origin, such as bird and insect wings) do not. Vestigial organs, such as the human appendix, are reduced remains.
- Example of selection: dark peppered moths became common in sooty industrial areas because birds ate the light ones that showed up on dark trees.

- Origin of life: Oparin and Haldane proposed that simple gases formed organic molecules; Miller and Urey (1953) made amino acids by passing sparks through methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour.
- Hardy-Weinberg: in a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation or migration, allele frequencies stay constant. p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
> In a population, 16 % of people show a recessive trait. What percentage are heterozygous carriers?
! Antibiotics do not cause resistance in bacteria. Resistant variants already exist; the drug kills the others, and the resistant ones multiply.
## Quick check
- Phenotype ratio of a monohybrid F₂? (3 : 1)
- Which blood group shows codominance? (AB)
- Chromosomes in a person with Down syndrome? (47)
- Which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments? (DNA ligase)
- Codons in the genetic code? (64)
- Forelimbs of a bat and a whale are which kind of organ? (homologous)
